title: Retrieval: Week Four
focus: Last retrieval day of the cycle. Every template from Days 22 to 27, blind, then the thirty problems.

cards.title: Arrays and Strings: blind recall
cards.trigger: Three of this week's six are 'prove it is linear' problems. That proof is the graded part.
cards.recall: Paper: the budget window, the run-start guard, the place-at-own-index swap, the carry-both-extremes update, the 3Sum duplicate skips, and the merge-and-count line. Then say the amortised argument for the three that need one.
template: # The three amortised-linear arguments you must be able to say:
#   longest consecutive : each run is walked once, from its unique start
#   first missing pos   : each swap places one value permanently
#   monotonic stack     : each index pushed once, popped once
# and the two duplicate-skip idioms, which are NOT the same:
if i > start and a[i] == a[i-1]: continue     # sibling skip, before choosing
while lo < hi and a[lo] == a[lo-1]: lo += 1   # after recording a match
keyInsights: Any time an inner loop is inside an outer loop and the answer is still linear, they will ask you to prove it. Have the sentence ready
Duplicate handling has two distinct idioms. Mixing them produces missing or repeated results
Merge sort is worth keeping sharp purely because counting during the merge unlocks a whole family
cards.trap: Claiming O(n) for longest consecutive without the start guard. The code without the guard is O(n^2) and looks identical at a glance.

cards.title: Structures and Design: blind recall
cards.trigger: Four design questions this week. All four are 'compose two structures so both operations are O(1)'.
cards.recall: From memory: the nested iterator's hasNext contract, the k-group three-pointer reconnection, LFU's three maps and min_freq rule, the freq-stack group insert, the BST iterator spine, and the calculator's parenthesis frame.
template: # The composition pattern behind LRU, LFU and FreqStack:
#   one map for O(1) LOOKUP
#   one ordered structure for O(1) ORDERING
#   one scalar tracking the current extreme, which only ever moves by one
# The bounded-scalar argument, stated once and reused three times:
#   min_freq / max_freq changes by exactly 1 per operation,
#   so it never needs a scan.
keyInsights: Three design questions share one skeleton. Learning the skeleton is cheaper than learning three solutions
The bounded-scalar argument is what turns an O(n) scan into O(1). It is the reusable idea in this whole lane
Iterator design is graded on the contract between hasNext and next, not on the traversal
cards.trap: Building LFU without resetting min_freq to 1 on insert. Every test with an eviction after a new key fails, and it is one line.

cards.title: Trees: blind recall
cards.trigger: The array techniques came to the trees this week. Prefix sums, greedy, and level linking without a queue.
cards.recall: From memory: the ancestor-carrying DFS, the BST straddle walk, the dummy-head level linker, the path collector with its copy and pop, the three-state camera greedy, and the tree prefix-sum with its undo.
template: # Five tree shapes now, complete:
#   1. push DOWN            preorder with carried state
#   2. pull UP              postorder returning an answer
#   3. pull UP + RECORD     the answer bends at a node
#   4. as an undirected GRAPH   parent map, then BFS
#   5. path ACCUMULATOR     running state + undo on the way out
# Shape 5 is shape 1 with a mutable accumulator, and the undo is what
# keeps sibling subtrees from seeing each other.
keyInsights: Five shapes cover every tree question in this program. Naming the shape first is faster than pattern-matching the problem
The undo line appears in path sum III, in backtracking, and in N-Queens. It is one habit, three problems
Greedy on a tree is always postorder, because you can only commit once you know what the children need
cards.trap: Putting the `path.pop()` inside the else branch of the leaf check. The recorded paths are correct and every path after the first is wrong.

cards.title: DP: blind recall
cards.trigger: Counting or optimising. Add or max. One word in the prompt picks the operator.
cards.recall: For all six: name the shape, say the state sentence, write the recurrence. Then say, for each, whether it counts or optimises, and which operator that implies.
template: # The operator rule:
#   'how many ways'   -> dp[..] += ...        (alternatives ADD)
#   'best / longest'  -> dp[..] = max(...)    (alternatives COMPETE)
#   'is it possible'  -> dp[..] = a or b      (alternatives OR)
# The loop-order rules, all four, one line each:
for c in range(cap, w-1, -1):   # 0/1 knapsack
for c in range(w, cap+1):       # unbounded knapsack
for coin in coins: ...          # combinations
for amount in ...: ...          # permutations
keyInsights: Counting versus optimising is a one-word read of the prompt and it decides the operator. Get it wrong and nothing else matters
Four loop-order rules cover the entire knapsack family. They are worth more drilling than any single problem
Direction of fill is a design decision. Choose whichever removes the boundary cases
cards.trap: Using max in a counting problem. It returns a plausible number and it is not the answer. Read the question word before writing the recurrence.

cards.title: Graphs: blind recall
cards.trigger: Two of this week's problems are solved by inverting the question. That is the transferable idea.
cards.recall: From memory: Kahn producing an order plus the heap variant, the DSU over string keys, the alien-dictionary first-difference rule, the uphill climb from the border, eight-direction BFS with enqueue-marking, and the border-anchored flood.
template: # Two inversions worth keeping:
#   'which cells reach X'      -> search FROM X, inverting the move rule
#   'which regions are closed' -> find the OPEN ones, everything else is closed
# And the modelling question that precedes every graph problem:
#   what is a node? what is an edge? is it directed? are weights involved?
# Four answers, and the algorithm follows.
keyInsights: Inverting the search direction turns quadratic into linear on two of this week's problems. Look for it whenever the question is 'which things can reach'
Modelling is the graded step in accounts merge and alien dictionary. The algorithm afterwards is one you already know
Marking on enqueue rather than dequeue is the one BFS habit that silently ruins complexity
cards.trap: Building an alien-dictionary edge for every position where the words differ. Only the first difference carries information, and the rest are fabricated constraints.
